abstracts.value: A search for dark matter particles is presented using events with large missing transverse momentum and a single energetic jet containing few constituents. The analysis uses proton-proton collision data recorded by the CMS experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. This corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$, recorded during the 2016$-$2018 LHC data-taking period. This is the first search at the LHC to employ the low-multiplicity jet signature. Supervised machine learning is used to maximize sensitivity to potential signals in this challenging final state. No excess of events over the standard model background prediction is observed. The results are used to set upper limits on the dark matter production cross section at 95% confidence level (CL) within simplified models featuring vector and axial-vector mediators. For a dark matter particle mass of approximately 150 (550) GeV, mediator masses up to 4250 (3500) GeV are excluded at 95% CL.

titles.title: Search for dark matter produced in association with a low-multiplicity jet in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV

abstracts.value: We explore the fundamental limits on finite-time driving in quantum critical systems described by boundary conformal field theory. We show that stochastic work fluctuations arising from external driving are a resource for speedy control, and derive an exact, saturable fluctuation-based speed limit in weakly driven boundary conformal field theories at finite temperature. The bound and saturating protocol can be expressed entirely in terms of the universal scaling dimension, and the result interpolates between the Kibble--Zurek regime,where temporal correlations are strongly nonlocal, and an adiabatic regime where linear driving becomes optimal. For small scaling dimension, the enhanced temporal correlations produce pronounced departures from linear protocols and a larger optimization advantage. These results establish a universal work precision--time tradeoff for boundary-critical control, applicable to quantum impurity, fractional quantum Hall, and superconducting-circuit platforms.

titles.title: Work fluctuation speed limit in boundary conformal field theories

abstracts.value: Spin qubits are an attractive platform for scalable quantum information processing, and recently, laterally gated quantum dots (QDs) in Ge heterostructures have emerged as a leading implementation of spin qubits. To date, RF single-hole transistors (SHT) and integrated superconducting resonators have been used for spin and charge readout, but their size can pose challenges. Here we demonstrate compact RF gate-dispersive charge readout of a Ge double QD (DQD), and a single hole box (SHB)-DQD system. We resolve QD loading and interdot transitions with both techniques. We find that the SHB enhances the interdot signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of our 540 MHz circuit by a factor of 20 for a DQD coupling $t_c \approx 5$ GHz, providing a unity-SNR at 135 microseconds, c.f. for 2.7 miliseconds for the direct detection. Power- and temperature-dependent measurements verify that SNR is limited by dielectric loss which compromises impedance matching. These results establish a compact readout approach based on gate-dispersive detection for Ge/SiGe heterostructure QDs.

titles.title: Gate Dispersive Charge Detection in Ge/SiGe Quantum Dots

abstracts.value: The next generation of telecommunication networks will rely on the distribution of complex quantum resources to enable secure and transformative information processing, utilizing entanglement and superposition. Cluster states-multi-qubit entangled states that retain entanglement under local measurements-are the central resource for measurement-based quantum information processing and compelling for quantum networking applications including blind quantum computing and quantum key agreement. However, transmitting cluster states over optical fiber has remained elusive with previous approaches, as losses scale exponentially with the number of photons. Here, we report the first transmission of a four-qubit cluster state to two parties over a partially deployed single-mode fiber link. The qubits of this state are encoded in two photons with multi-level time-bins. We directly generate the cluster state by exploiting coherent control of a parametric generation process, rendering a resource-intensive controlled-phase gate obsolete. To enable processing of this state, we introduce beam splitting for time-bins via chirped pulse modulation-a novel, reconfigurable Fourier-domain pulse shaping technique. We certify genuine multi-qubit entanglement and demonstrate one-way computing primitives on the transmitted cluster state. Our approach achieves the transmission of cluster states over optical fiber, establishing complex quantum resources fully compatible with telecommunication infrastructure.

titles.title: Transmission of multi-level time-bin encoded cluster states over 29 km of partially deployed optical fiber

abstracts.value: A search for charged-lepton-flavour violation (cLFV) in top-quark production and decay is presented. The data analysed correspond to 140 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions recorded at a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}= 13$ TeV by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The possible cLFV contribution is studied via two mechanisms. The first is via the production of a leptonically-decaying single-top quark in association with a pair of oppositely-charged different-flavour leptons. The second is the production of top-quark pairs, where one top quark decays into a pair of oppositely-charged different-flavour leptons and a $u$- or $c$-quark, while the other decays into a leptonically-decaying $W$ boson and a $b$-quark, according to the Standard Model. The signal processes contain three charged leptons, taken to be electrons or muons. No significant deviation from the Standard Model prediction is observed, and these results are interpreted within an Effective Field Theory framework. Upper limits are placed at 95% confidence level on six Wilson coefficients, ranging from $|C^{\mathrm{tensor}}_{eμtu}|/Λ^2 < 0.018$ TeV$^{-2}$ to $|C^{\mathrm{scalar}}_{eμtc}|/Λ^2 < 0.32$ TeV$^{-2}$ for the tensor $u$-quark and scalar $c$-quark couplings, respectively. These Wilson coefficient limits are translated into 95% confidence level upper limits on cLFV top-quark decay branching ratios, ranging from $B(t \to eμu) < 6 \cdot 10^{-9}$ to $B(t \to eμc) < 2.7 \cdot 10^{-7}$ for the scalar $u$-quark and tensor $c$-quark couplings, respectively.

titles.title: Search for charged-lepton-flavour violating $eμtq$ interactions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV with the ATLAS detector

abstracts.value: We develop a continuum counts-in-cells fluctuation theory for gravitational clustering in galaxy populations described by a continuous comoving mass function $\phi (m,z)$ within the quasi-equilibrium grand-canonical framework. Starting from the equal-mass and two-species fluctuation sectors, we construct a finite-resolution mass-bin representation, pass to the continuum limit and derive closed expressions for the internal energy, the pressure, and the first four count cumulants in the strict total-count sector. The latter is then rewritten in an intrinsic normalization based on the mean mass $\bar{m} = M_1/M_0$, so that the observable hierarchy depends only on the mass function, the clustering parameter, and the thermodynamic control variables. The continuum construction recovers the equal-mass formulas exactly and reproduces the discrete two-species relations in the corresponding singular limit. In the weak-clustering regime, the leading spectral corrections are controlled by the moments $M_3$, $M_6$, and $M_9$. Within the strict total-count criticality condition, the compressibility denominator is pinned to $D_c=1/2$, so the Fano factor takes the fixed value $F_c=2$ as an algebraic identity that follows directly from the criticality condition, whereas the higher reduced cumulants preserve explicit dependence on the mass spectrum through the response hierarchy $A_r$. A truncated Schechter specialization for threshold-selected catalogs then makes the physical content explicit: raising the lower mass threshold lowers the critical clustering parameter while increasing the variance-, skewness-, and kurtosis-level responses of the counts-in-cells distribution. The resulting framework furnishes an analytical interface between quasi-equilibrium gravitational clustering theory and finite-resolution mass-selected one-point observables for realistic galaxy populations.

titles.title: Generalized Fluctuation Theory of Galaxy Clustering With Continuous Mass Spectra

Statement of Contributions

This thesis is based on the arXiv preprint Chutes and Ladders: Dynamical Automor-
phisms via the ZX-calculus [1]. Sascha Zakaib-Bernier and Dr. Alexander Frei are joint-first
authors, while Zach Mann, Dr. Michael Vasmer, and Prof. Victor V. Albert are co-authors.
The author of this thesis contributed to the writing and the development of the formalism,
proofs and protocols found in the Letter [1] with her joint-first author Dr. Frei. They ben-
efited from the support and advice from the co-authors. MSc Mann helped to compute the
LC orbits of the codes used in subsection 4.2.4, and edited the preprint. Dr. Vasmer and
Prof. Albert helped with some numerical simulations to compute the code automorphism
group in subsection 4.2.4 as well as editing the preprint.

Portions of chapter 1, subsection 2.2.4, section 2.4, section 2.5, chapter 4, and chapter
5 are modified from and overlap with the preprint. The portions that overlap between the
two bodies of work were written by the author of this thesis and edited by the co-authors.

iii



Abstract

Quantum error correction enables the protection of quantum information from noise
arising from imperfect control and unwanted interactions with the environment. Manip-
ulating logical information in quantum error-correcting codes remains challenging, as we
can only directly access physical qubits, not the encoded logical qubits. In fact, we know
it is not possible to get the full logical universal gate set by doing transversal physical
operations. As a solution to this problem, many schemes for implementing encoded log-
ical gates have been developed, including dynamical automorphism gates (DA). These
logical protocols are realized by measurement sequences that transfer logical information
between different codespaces. In parallel, there has been a growing interest in the intersec-
tion between quantum error correction and the ZX-calculus, a graphical representation of
quantum processes. This direction has proved to be fruitful. For example, it has allowed
the development of new dynamical codes. However, logic within such codes has not yet
been tackled. In this thesis, we offer a formalism for dynamical automorphisms based
on the ZX-calculus, implementing logical Clifford gates for stabilizer codes. We begin by
defining the basics of quantum information, the stabilizer formalism and the ZX-calculus.
Then, we build upon this formalism for gauge fixing via the ZX-calculus. Since gauge fixing
may be implemented via measurement, our formalism allows us to protocols implementing
dynamical automorphisms. In particular, we start by investigating a DA for a 3-qubit mo-
tivating code and its LC orbit. Then, we turn to an example of a logical CZ for the [[4, 2, 2]]
code. Finally, we show an example of a distance-preserving dynamical automorphism for
the [[7, 1, 3]] bare code implementing a phase gate, which was inaccessible using previous
techniques.

Chapter 1

Introduction

Quantum information promises computations that are intractable with classical computers
and communication in a way that allows eavesdroppers to be detected [2]. Despite these
promises, quantum technologies are still in their infancy. The main reason for this is the
fragility of quantum information; slight perturbations due to the environment can destroy
quantum advantages. Quantum error correction (QEC) is an essential step toward scalable
quantum computing, as it encodes logical information across many physical qubits in a sub-
space where errors can be detected and corrected. Recent experiments have demonstrated
QEC across various platforms, including superconducting qubits [3–7], trapped ions [8–12],
and neutral atoms [13, 14].

While there is still room for improvement in the hardware and QEC techniques, the
next step is performing fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. The standard approach is to
decompose an algorithm into a small number of quantum gates forming a universal set [2],
and then to design fault-tolerant implementations of these gates in a given QEC code.
Transversal gates [15] have a tensor-product structure and are therefore naturally fault
tolerant, but no QEC code possesses a universal and transversal set of logical gates [16].
As a result, for any QEC code, at least one logical gate must be implemented using a
more complex fault-tolerant scheme, such as, e.g. lattice surgery [17–22], magic state
distillation [23–27], and code-switching [28–32]. Even so, no consensus yet exists on how
to best perform the logical operations necessary to compute any quantum algorithm fault-
tolerantly.

The usual QEC paradigm is to encode the logical information into a single subspace:
the codespace. However, recent proposals have explored QEC techniques where the system
is dynamically driven between different codespaces [33–37]. These dynamical codes enable

1



QEC using lower-weight measurements, and can also be used to implement logical Clifford
gates [38].

Creating dynamical codes out of static codes requires flexibility in terms of resources and
depth of the QEC circuits. Decoding also becomes less straightforward when transitioning
from a subspace to another. Many have thus turned to the ZX-calculus [39–41], a graphical
representation of quantum circuits, to describe these types of protocols.

The ZX-calculus has proved to be useful for perfecting QEC protocols in many instances,
mostly for its optimization strengths and ease of interpretation: QEC codes have been
translated into the ZX-calculus [42, 43], allowing us to construct new codes [44, 45], and to
perform lattice surgery [46] and other techniques [47, 48] to generate logic in QEC codes.
Also, Pauli webs, emerging from the ZX-calculus, form detecting regions, which inform
us of the measurements needed to detect errors in particular circuits [37]. Furthermore,
a lot of space-time, Floquet and dynamical codes have emerged from the ZX-calculus
representation [49–53].

In this thesis, we develop a ZX-calculus–based formalism for dynamical automorphisms
for the implementation of logical Clifford gates. Complementing prior ZX-calculus appli-
cations that address the construction of dynamical codes [33, 34, 37, 53–55], we leverage
ZX-calculus to design and implement their automorphisms. We expect that the machine-
interpretability of this formalism will facilitate the search for new dynamical codes and
logical gates.

The key ingredient of our approach is a ZX-calculus representation of gauge fixing [29,
56], a technique to transfer encoded information between stabilizer codes via measurement-
based shortcuts, which may fault-tolerantly implement high depth unitary circuits. We give
three examples of dynamical automorphisms via gauge fixing: the logical Clifford group
for a [[3, 1]] motivating code, an entangling logical CZ gate for the error-detecting [[4, 2, 2]]
code, and a logical phase gate for the error-correcting [[7, 1, 3]] bare code [57].

This manuscript is structured as follows. First, we lay the foundations for the results in
chapter 2. We introduce the basics of quantum information, stabilizer formalism, stabilizer
codes, the ZX-calculus, and finally stabilizer codes represented in the ZX-calculus. Next,
chapter 3 reviews some well-known protocols for fault-tolerant logical gates, such as magic
state distillation, lattice surgery, code automorphisms and dynamical automorphisms. This
will lead us into the results, i.e. dynamical automorphisms via the ZX-calculus. Chapter
4 first explains gauge fixing in the ZX-calculus before giving the concrete examples of
dynamical automorphisms listed above. Finally, chapter 5 closes off this manuscript with
a discussion of the results, future work, and comparisons with other protocols.

2.1 Introduction to Quantum Information Principles

In quantum error correction, we aim to encode a k-qubit quantum state into a larger space
of n-qubits in a way that we can correct and detect errors due to noise. The process is
illustrated by the circuit in figure 2.1: the encoding map E projects the logical state and
the ancilla |ψ⟩ ⊗ |0⟩⊗m into |ψℓ⟩. Once protected, the qubits may undergo some known
noise N , and the recovery map R decodes and corrects the logical information. Each map
brings a quantum state to another, i.e. they are channels. The goal of this section is
to introduce all the relevant information to understand QEC encoding maps as quantum
channels. Before defining them, we introduce some of the notation used to describe quan-
tum states. We will end this section by introducing representations of quantum channels:
the Choi-representation of a quantum channel, and the Kraus representation. For a com-
plete introduction to quantum information, we refer the reader to John Watrous’s book,
The Theory of Quantum Information [58], on which this section is based.

2.1.2 Quantum Channels

Quantum channels, or simply channels, are a subset of linear maps of operators Φ, denoted
by the set

T(X ,Y) = {Φ : L(X ) → L(Y)}, (2.7)

with specific properties. We first introduce positive maps, which send positive operators
to positive operators.

Definition 4 ([58]). A map Φ ∈ T(X ,Y) is positive if Φ(P ) ∈ Pos(Y) for every P ∈
Pos(X ).

This allows us to understand completely positive maps.

Definition 5 ([58]). A map Φ is completely positive (CP) if Φ⊗ 1L(Z) is positive for all
complex Euclidean spaces Z.

This definition may seem redundant comparatively to positive maps, but there exist
positive maps that are not completely positive, notably the transpose map. This means

6



that taking the partial transpose of a bipartite state ρ ∈ D(X ⊗ Y) could produce send
the initial density matrix outside of D(X ⊗ Y) ⊆ L(X ⊗ Y)1. These types of map aren’t
channels, as they don’t send all quantum states to other quantum states.

Finally, we need one last type of map to define channels, i.e. trace-preserving maps.

Definition 6 ([58]). A map Φ ∈ T(X ,Y) is trace-preserving (TP) if Tr(Φ(X))= Tr(X)
for all X ∈ L(X ).

A TP map will thus send a density operator to another operator σ with trace equal to
1. For σ to be in D(Y), it needs to also be in Pos(Y), so the map needs to also be CP. So
we conclude that a quantum channel is a CPTP map and vice versa.

Definition 7 ([58]). A quantum channel is a linear map Φ : L(X ) → L(Y) for some choice
of complex Euclidean spaces X & Y, satisfying two properties:

1. Completely positive,

2. Trace-preserving.

We denote the set of quantum channels, or CPTP maps, as CPTP(X ,Y).

2.3 Stabilizer codes

As a means of introducing QEC codes, we first take a look at a classical 3-bit repetition code
in subsection 2.3.1, and then to the 3-qubit repetition code in subsection 2.3.2. This will
lead us to discuss the noise channels that create the errors we want to correct in. Finally
we will define stabilizer codes in subsection 2.3.4, subsystem codes where we introduce
gauge fixing 2.3.5, and dynamical codes 2.3.6. For subsections (2.3.1-2.3.2, 2.3.4), we take
inspiration from Gottesman’s An Introduction to Quantum Error Correction and Fault-
Tolerant Quantum Computation [60].

2.3.1 3-bit Repetition Code

In a classical computer, information is stored in bits. An error presents itself as a bit
flip with probability p. We may assume that the noise is independent and identically
distributed, i.i.d. noise. To correct errors in this noise model, the 3-bit repetition strategy
is to copy every bit b ∈ {0, 1} 3 times. So with figure 2.1 in mind,3 the encoding is
E(b) = bbb ∈ {000, 111}. After the bits have gone through a noise channel N ,the logical
information can be recovered R ◦N (⌊⌊⌊) by measuring all bits and taking the majority
vote as the outcome bit b′. This decoding strategy bets that the errors are small and so
most bits didn’t flip, meaning b′ = b. The probability of the majority being wrong is
pwrong = p3+p2(1−p). So, this scheme exhibits a quadratic suppression of error rates from
p 7→ p2.

2.3.3 Quantum Error Models

To understand how to correct noise in a quantum computer, we first need to describe it.
There are many possible models to describe noise in quantum systems. It can be i.i.d.,
coherent [76], biased [77], correlated [78], non-Markovian where the environment retains
memory of past operations [79], qubit loss [80], leakage into higher energy states [81], and
circuit-level [82]. The former considers noise on every element in your circuit, from state
preparation to gates and to measurements, so it is a corner stone of noise estimation in
QEC.

Different QEC codes perform better under different types of noise. For the purpose of
this work, we will only go over the depolarizing channel, an i.i.d. noise model that can be
decomposed in terms of Pauli operators. As such, it lends itself well to stabilizer QEC.

Because in stabilizer QEC, we measure stabilizers expressed as Pauli strings to find
syndromes and correct errors, we effectively decompose and discretize errors into the Pauli

2.3.4 Stabilizer Codes: Definition and Examples

An n-qubit stabilizer code [15, 65] is specified by an Abelian subgroup of the n-qubit
Pauli group that does not contain −I, i.e. the stabilizer group S = {s1, s2, . . . , sm}.
The states that are in the codespace made up of the stabilizers are called codewords.
Since the complex Euclidean space of the physical qubits holds the stabilizer and logical
degrees of freedom, the code k = n −m logical qubits. Each logical qubit is represented
by sets of anticommuting logical operators {Xℓ, Zℓ} that commute with S, but are not
contained within it. In other words the logical operators of the code are in N(S)/S, where
N(S) = {P ∈ Pn|PSP ∗ = S} is the normalizer of the group. As such, stabilizers are
sometimes called the centre of the code, since they commute with each other and all the
logical operators. The logical operators map between different codewords, which are all in
the codespace and thus protected from the noise.

The tolerance of error correction codes is described by the code distance d = 2t + 1,
where t is the number of errors tolerated. The code distance comes from classical coding
theory and is defined as the minimum weight of a logical Pauli operator.5 This is because it
represents the number of Pauli operators needed to map to each other two elements of the
codespace, the space spanned by the stabilizers. We refer to the minimum weight because
a given representative of the logical operator is equivalent to another up to stabilizers. In
the case of the 3-qubit repetition code, 3 bit flips (Xℓ) mapped the logical |0ℓ⟩ to |1ℓ⟩,
meaning d = 3. This matches with the previous conclusion that a only single bit-flip error
can be corrected using that code.

Stabilizer codes are denoted using the shorthand [[n, k, d]], where d is the code distance.
In contrast, classical codes are denoted using simple brackets [n, k, d]. When d = 2, this
means the code can only detect single-qubit errors, and a d = 1 code doesn’t achieve any
error correction.

The information about a stabilizer code can be compactly written in many ways. In the
symplectic representation, the stabilizers can be put into a binary matrix H = (SX |SZ),
where the rows span the stabilizers and the entries are the X(Z) support of each stabilizer
on the right(left) side of the matrix [65]. This matrix is often called the parity check
matrix, a term coming from classical coding theory. For example, we list the stabilizers of
the 5-qubit code [83] and the stabilizer matrix in symplectic representation.

Another useful example to note is CSS codes [84, 85]. Their stabilizers are either made
of Z Pauli strings or X Pauli strings. Then, the stabilizers are called Z-type or X-type.

We close off this long, but important subsection with an overview of the stabilizer
QEC process: logical information is encoded into a QEC code’s codespace |ψℓ⟩ using
multiple physical qubits. It experiences noise N which may be modelled as applying
Pauli operators to the physical qubits with a small probability p. Then, the stabilizers
of the code are measured to obtain the syndromes. The circuits designed for this step
are called syndrome extraction circuits. From the syndrome information, a possible error
is diagnosed and can be corrected by applying some Pauli operators onto our physical
qubits. Before measuring the stabilizers and applying a correction, there may be some
quantum computation performed, which will be explored in Chapter 3. All this enables
the protection of our logical qubits.

The process of finding the appropriate correction for given syndromes is called decoding.
Different QEC codes call for different decoding strategies or algorithms. In general, this
problem is NP-hard [95], implying that it is unlikely there exists a polynomial-time algo-
rithm that can decode a QEC code. Even more so, finding an optimal decoding algorithm
is #-P hard, so it is harder than decoding classical codes [96]. However, it is possible to
choose our encoding carefully such that decoding is possible. Many schemes have been
devised over the years, notably minimum weight perfect matching decoders for topological
codes [82, 97] and tensor network-based maximum likelihood decoders [98].

2.3.5 Subsystem codes

In subsystem codes [56], the codespace of a stabilizer code is separated into two subsystems
C = A⊗B. In the first subspace A, the logical information ρA ∈ B(A) is stored, while the
second subspace B remains a degree of freedom. More concretely, this means that some
of the logical qubits in C become labelled as gauge qubits ρB ∈ B(B). If r qubits become
gauge qubits, the code is denoted by the four variables [[n, k, r, d]].

Gauge is an overloaded word, so what does it mean here? Two codewords ρa ⊗ ρB and
ρa⊗ρ′B hold the same information even if ρB ̸= ρ′B, implying they are connected by a gauge
transformation. This transformation can be defined by a set of gauge operators g ∈ G that
map through conjugation the gauge states to each other gρbg∗ = ρ′B. This behaviour might
ring a bell: the gauge operators act on the gauge subspace like the logical operators do
on the logical codewords. So, they are the gauge’s old logical operators, and we use the
notation {Xg, Zg} instead of g from now on.

After removing a few qubits from their lot, the logical operators {Xℓ, Zℓ} are now in

The gauge qubits, since they hold no information, can be used as a fault-tolerant
resource for different QEC protocols. For example, they can enable simpler recovery pro-

is at the centre of the work presented in this manuscript [1]. In practice, gauge fixing may
be realized by measuring the logical operators associated with a given state.

The gauge qubit’s states can be fixed by measuring one of its gauge operators: Xg, Yg or
ZG will project the qubit into their respective ±1 eigenstates. Depending on the procedure
at hand, there may be a correction necessary to get the correct eigenvalue, but this may
always be done by classical bookkeeping. Effectively, by projecting into the eigenbasis of
a gauge operator, gauge fixing promotes that operator to become part of the centre of the
code, i.e. the stabilizers [102].

Gauge fixing reduces the dimensions of the subsystem B, and enlarges S, but the flow
can go in the other direction too. To create a subsystem code from a stabilizer code, one
of its stabilizers may be demoted by convention to become a gauge operator Zg. There
still needs another Pauli string to form an anticommuting set. The destabilizers [94] lends
itself perfectly for this purpose. Every destabilizer is a Pauli string that commutes with all
but one stabilizer. With the stabilizers, they form a complete basis for Pn. Coming back
to gauge qubits, to create more of them, one can demote a stabilizer to become Zg and its
destabilizer to become Xg.

To summarize, subsystem codes are stabilizer codes that have gauge qubits in which
no information is stored. They may be used to connect different stabilizer codes through
gauge fixing.8 Information in logical qubits may be transferred from one encoding to

It is worth mentioning that subsystem codes may not be exclusively used as bridges
between stabilizer codes. In fact, they were first introduced as a way to facilitate decoding
with the Bacon-Shor code [100], to better absorb errors [105] or to reduce the weight of
the measurement performed to collect syndromes [101].

2.3.6 Dynamical Codes

Stabilizer codes presented so far have been static: the logical information is encoded into
the codespace associated with a given QEC code. Now that we understand how to switch
between codes, one may wonder: why stay confined within a single code? Different codes
have different properties, so it could be useful to exploit complementary ones, as will be
explored in section 3.5. Also, as mentioned at the end of the last subsection, playing with

8This may also be called code switching, but we refrain from discussing it in this section because it was
originally introduced in the context of logical gates. As such, we will discuss them further in section 3.5.

27



different measurement schedules than the direct syndrome measurements may allow you
to facilitate state recovery or to make the measurements needed to get syndromes easier.

Dynamical codes represent this new paradigm where we let the code evolve in time based
on a measurement schedule. At each time step, there is an instantaneous stabilizer code
generated by the stabilizers and the gauge operators that were just measured. This scheme,
proposed by Hastings and Haah [33], attracted a lot of attention recently. In their work,
the authors exploit a parent subsystem code and the logical information flows between
three child codes. Interestingly, the parent subsystem can’t hold any logical information,
meaning that if treated statically, any of the three child stabilizer codes also holds no logical
qubits. However, a well-crafted gauge measurement schedule between the three stabilizer
codes allows us to create 2 logical qubits.

To understand this measurement schedule, we first point to the code construction il-
lustrated in figure 2.7a. The qubits are on a hexagonal lattice, which is 3-colourable. If
the lattice has n plaquettes, or face, then there are 2n physical qubits and 3n edges. Each
edge represents a 2-qubit gauge operator. At a given vertex, three edges meet and they all
represent anticommuting 2-qubit Pauli operators. Each plaquette represents a stabilizer
by taking the product of the operators on its border. With two stabilizers that span the
length of the periodic space, the stabilizer group is of dimension n+ 1. Now we can count
the number of gauge qubits as the number of independent anticommuting sets of 2-qubit
Pauli operators (3n−1)/29 without the centre stabilizers, so (3n−1− (2n−1))/2 = n−1.

However, a measurement schedule can be created where all the gauge operators of
colour c are measured at once in a periodic loop: red, green, blue, red, green blue, etc.
This periodic sequence is illustrated in figure 2.7b, where the logical operators get updated
up to a stabilizer of the previous code as in the gauge fixing example of subsection 2.3.5.
We mention that the actual period of this code involves 6 measurements and not 3, as the
figure suggests, because each round generates a -1 sign. However, we work in the symplectic
representation, so this phase difference is ignored.

After the first period of measurements, we have enough information such that the in-
stantaneous stabilizer code may be defined. Since the subset of c gauge operators has
disjoint support on the qubits, the operators all commute with each other. Their mea-
surements promote them to become stabilizers. This code has n plaquettes and n c gauge
operators, but the product of all plaquettes and the product of all c gauge operators with c
coloured plaquettes are both 1. So the stabilizer group is of dimension 2n− 2. This means
that there are k = n−m− g = 2n− (2n− 2) = 2 logical qubits.

2.5 Stabilizer Codes in the ZX-Calculus

Now, we assemble all the background information to represent stabilizer codes in the ZX-
calculus, i.e. as ZX-encoding graphs. The latter will be defined first in subsection 2.5.1.
Next, subsection 2.5.2 discusses the bijection called map-state duality between ZX-encoding
graphs and stabilizer states, which correspond to graph states and local Clifford gates. This
allows us to use the LC equivalence on ZX-encoding graphs and find the stabilizer code
they represent in subsection 2.5.3. Then, in subsection 2.5.4, we explain how to construct
the ZX-encoding graph given a set of stabilizers and logical operators. Finally, we discuss
the existence of a normal form for ZX-encoding graphs and how to obtain it in subsection
2.5.5.

2.5.1 ZX-Encoding Graphs

In the ZX-calculus, stabilizer codes are represented by their encoder, i.e. by Clifford
isometries called ZX-encoding graphs. Starting from the encoding circuit of a stabilizer
code, its ZX-encoding graph may be constructed by translating each gate in the ZX-calculus
to find the equivalent ZX-diagram, and simplifying the ZX-diagram into a graph-like ZX-
diagram with some local Clifford operators on input or output wires [107, theorem 5.4]. It
is also possible to build the graph from the stabilizers and the logical operators, as will be
explained in subsection 2.5.4.

To define ZX-encoding graphs, we take inspiration from previous work [42, 44, 45].

Definition 11. A ZX-encoding graph is a bipartite graph-like ZX-diagram, where the bi-
adjacency matrix is full rank and 1-qubit local Clifford gates can be added to the input or
output wires.

We highlight that this includes subsystem codes: a logical input may simply be rela-
belled as a gauge input. From now on, we will choose to only consider a single gauge qubit
at a time for simplicity. In any case, the gauge qubits are only measured one at a time in
dynamical codes and dynamical automorphisms.

Via the map-state duality, it is possible to associate a given ZX-encoding graph with a sta-

So far, QEC has been discussed in the context of a quantum memory: logical information
is encoded, experiences noise, and gets corrected according to stabilizer measurements. To
perform quantum computation on the information within a QEC code, we turn to active
QEC as illustrated in figure 3.1.

Figure 3.1: Active QEC protocol. The state |ψ⟩ holding k logical qubits is encoded into the

Because logical qubits are not directly accessible, finding protocols G to generate logical
gates without corrupting the logical information is often hard. We’d like to avoid perform-
ing gates which "badly spread" errors. For example, performing a CNOT gate between two
physical qubits could spread what was a single-qubit Pauli error into two-qubit errors (see
equation (2.70)). Since a QEC code [[n, k, d]] only tolerates t = (d − 1)/2 errors, this bad
propagation of error may cause a correctable error to become uncorrectable, thus putting
at risk the logical information.

More generally, every step, or gadget, described in figure 3.1 will be implemented
imperfectly in some way or another, and may jeopardize the whole QEC protocol. Even
the noise channel is only a model of the actual noise present in a quantum computer, and
thus imperfectly represent the system.

A big piece of the puzzle that has been overlooked so far in this manuscript, but is worth
mentioning, is decoding. The recovery map presented in subsection 2.3.2 was somewhat
straightforward, but for a general stabilizer code, optimally decoding is #P problem [96],
meaning this task is much harder than for classical linear codes. As it was alluded to,

47



different decoding algorithms will have different performance since they might not catch
the same sets of errors. Thus, different noise models may affect the performance too.

Protocols that allow for quantum computation with logical qubits even with errors
acting on the gadgets are called fault-tolerant (FT). For a quantum computer to be FT,
every gadget has to work in synergy with the others. Using FT gadgets, it is possible
to suppress the logical error arbitrarily low by scaling up or concatenating QEC codes, if
the physical error rate p is under a certain threshold value p < pth. This is comes from
the threshold theorem [106, 112, 113] that states it may be realizable to construct good
enough FT quantum computers capable of useful computation, if the resources are good
enough. Many experiments have shown signs that scaling is possible with state-of-the-art
qubit control [5–7, 14].

According to their nature, different gadgets have different requirements to be considered
FT. The gadgets we will be discussing in this chapter are FT logical gates G. These FT
gates transform a correctable error into another correctable error by definition. For a single
code block encoded into a code with distance d correcting t errors, if the gate may generate
an error s and the state has an incoming error e1, then the error after the gate must be
e1 + s ≤ t. For gates involving two logical qubits encoded in the same code block, the
same rule applies. However, it’s a different story when two logical qubits are encoded in
two code blocks each capable of correcting t errors. Then, if e1 e2 are the incoming errors
on each qubit and s is the error generated by the 2-qubit gate for each qubit, an FT gate
must respect e1+e2+s ≤ t for each code block. So errors can be leaked from another code
block onto a given code block if the resulting error stays under that code block’s capacity.

The word fault-tolerance is often thrown around without a proper definition. Here
we offered a description that, although not complete, will be sufficient in the context
of this manuscript. For a rigorous explanation of fault-tolerance we refer the reader to
Gottesman’s book on the subject Surviving as a Quantum Computer in a Classical World
[114].

Transversal gates are the most straightforward way to build FT gates. While their
definition may vary between source, we will follow Nielsen and Chuang’s [115] definition:
transversal gates are gates that are implemented by independent physical gates affecting
a single qubit per code patch at a time. Often, the logical gate will be implemented by
broadcasting a gate across the physical qubits. As such, they are trivially fault-tolerant.
For example, the surface code introduced in Subsection 3.3.1 has a transversal H gate
implemented by broadcasting H across all qubits. It also has a transversal CNOT between
two code patches.1 Because each CNOT is supported on a single qubit in a code patch,

3.2 Magic State Distillation

Magic state distillation was introduced by Bravyi and Kitaev [24] as a scheme to generate
a fault-tolerant universal gate set by distilling magic states used to teleport a non-Clifford
gate onto a logical qubit. In the context of magic state distillation, it is assumed that the
lab has access to ideal Clifford gates, |0⟩ state preparation, and perfect Pauli measurements
[24].

Here, we will follow Gottesman’s introduction to magic state distillation [114]. There
are many different distillation protocols, but we focus on the one based on the 15-qubit
Reed-Muller code [24, 116, 117]. The basic idea is to encode noisy magic states into QEC
codes that have a transversal non-Clifford gate, measure the syndromes and discard the
states if they are non-trivial. The outcome can be decoded to get a single "purer" magic
state. Once we have achieved the desirable accuracy, the distilled state is encoded into the
QEC code that lacks the non-Clifford gate, and a magic state injection is performed to
transfer the gate from our magic state onto a logical qubit.

As mentioned above, magic states are the states used for magic state injection. This
definition is vague, so we try to make it clearer by illustrating in figure 3.2 the T state,
the magic state used below to generate T gates. In this rendering, the state is outside
the volume covered by Clifford operations from a Pauli eigenstate [24]. All such states are
often called magic states. However, not all those states are good for magic state injection.

It now becomes clear why there is such a big resource overhead: for each increment in
fidelity for a single magic state, the scheme processes 15 · 9 = 135 qubits, or even more
for a higher surface code distance achieving better fidelity. Also, each time the protocol is
applied, there is a probability that the syndromes measured are non-trivial, so everything
needs to be started over, including all the previous rounds of distillation.

3.2.3 Contributions and Outlooks

The first scheme developed to generate a fault-tolerant universal gate set is not magic
state distillation, but Shor’s Toffoli state preparation using cat states in 1996 [119]. Also,

53



Knill, Laflamme and Zurek [116] propose to use a code that has transversal CNOT and
T , and get the missing H gate by a procedure similar to the state injection presented
above. However, Bravyi and Kitaev’s magic state distillation offered a procedure to fault-
tolerantly realize any non-Clifford gate using Clifford gates and basic state preparation,
and they characterized which states are necessary to achieve this.

The magic state distillation’s assumptions might seem a bit contrived, since it assumes
access to ideal Clifford gates. However, the surface code has access to FT transversal
Clifford gates,3 so the only computation missing is a non-Clifford gate. The prevalence of
magic state distillation is thus associated with the rise of surface codes. As for the other two
assumptions, almost perfect state preparation of an initial |0⟩⊗n may be reasonable, but
perfect measurement of Pauli operators may be rather hard to achieve, even approximately,
depending on the implementation. That being said, syndrome extraction circuits may be
optimized to consider measurement errors [120].

Magic state distillation has its advantages and drawbacks. The distillation scheme itself
can be done separately from the logical information, which further protects it from our noisy
computations. However, a major drawback of this procedure is resource overhead. Magic
state distillation dominates resource estimations for the whole of FTQC. So effectively, the
non-Clifford gates become bottlenecks in quantum computation. Since Clifford circuits can
be simulated classically [15, 94], being able to compute non-Clifford gates is an essential
step towards quantum advantage. The strain on the production of magic states can be
alleviated by making magic state factories [82]. This architecture choice means there should
always be a magic state readily available for quantum computation, but it requires a lot
of resource overhead.

Up to this day, there is ongoing research to optimize the resource overhead of magic state
distillation, and its resource estimate has dropped [27]. For example, it can be minimized
by replacing the encoding of the 15 qubits with the Bivariate Bicycle code [121], a code
which has a high threshold and low overhead, instead of the surface code [122]. A really
promising different approach was optimized by Gidney et al. [123] in 2024 called magic
state cultivation, which we discuss below.

3.2.4 Magic State Cultivation

As the name suggests, magic state cultivation [123] protocols make the encoded states grow.
The basic structure of the magic state cultivation protocol is the following: start distillation

3See Section 3.3.

54



using small codes with a transversal T to initialize the magic states, and then grow it into
bigger and better codes until the desired accuracy is obtained. Thus, the protocol can
be separated into three stages: injection, cultivation, and escape. After elaborating the
protocols, they are simulated and with circuit-level depolarizing noise with an error rate
of 10−3. They estimate that they reduce the resources required to achieve accuracy of the
order of 10−9 by an order of magnitude compared to previous work. They also gain 2
orders of magnitude in accuracy by cutting the error rate in half.

First comes the injection stage. In their work, the authors explore three different ways
to initialize Tℓ |+ℓ⟩ in the d = 3 3D colour code [88], which has a transversal T gate [124].
They find that a "unitary injection" circuit performs best. This circuit is not a standard
encoding circuit of the colour code because it initializes the T magic state at a point where
the state is protected from Z errors.

The next goal is to grow the code to increase fault tolerance, i.e. the cultivation stage.
It contains 3 steps: check, grow and stabilize. In the check steps, we check the parity
of the state. So a T ∗

ℓ is applied to get |+ℓ⟩ state, and then the X parity is measured in
the +1 eigenspace of the SWAP operator and verified using time-reversed parity checks.
The Grow step consists of preparing the new physical qubits in Bell pairs, arranged in the
continuation of the hexagonal lattice typical of colour codes. To connect the new qubits, a
subset of stabilizers is measured.4 In the Stabilize step, three colour code cycles [125] are
performed to make sure the glue sticks.

The final step is the escape stage. Pretty quickly, growing the colour code becomes
infeasible with current decoders. So growing the code lowers the number of faults, but it
doesn’t increase the code distance. As such, the code needs to grow into a code that’s easier
to decode: the surface code. Since the colour codes and the surface codes lie on different
tessellations, i.e. a hexagonal lattice and a square lattice, this isn’t straightforward, and
previous work proved to be insufficiently efficient. Thus, the authors construct their own
method: they first grow the colour code into a surface code with one of its corners "folded"
onto itself, which they call the grafted code. This triangular section of the code corresponds
to the old colour code. Once they have the grafted code, decoding becomes much easier,
so now the state is protected by a QEC code with a bigger code distance than the initial
d = 3. However, the code distance may account for smaller error strings than what the
grown colour could do. They create a new code by merging some stabilizers from the colour
and surface code in a way that maximizes the tolerance for faults and the code distance.

In the paper, the authors describe the decoding procedures for each step. While decod-

3.3 Lattice Surgery

Magic is a staple of FTQC, but that’s not the end of the picture. It has been proved that
no QEC code has the full transversal Clifford group for more than a single qubit [126]. So
it becomes essential to consider FT protocols for Clifford gates. Lattice surgery answers
this question for a particular class of QEC codes.

Lattice surgery was first proposed by Horsman et al [17] as a tool to create FT protocols
for performing CNOTs on surface code blocks, or patches, with a 2D layout and only nearest
neighbour interactions.

In this section, we first introduce the surface code, and its transversal gates. Then,
based on [17, 99, 127], we explain lattice merging and splitting operations, the FT CNOT
procedure, and the S gate procedure. We finish off this section by going over the contri-
butions and outlooks of this work.

3.3.1 Primer on the Surface Code

The surface code [86, 87] is a CSS and QLDPC code defined on a planar square lattice.
The qubits can either lie on the vertices of the lattice or on the edges. Here, we place the
qubits on the vertices of the grid, as shown in figure 3.4. Thus, we present the rotated
surface code that has a better scaling [[d2, 1, d]] [17]. The stabilizers are then placed on
the faces of the lattice. The X and Z-type stabilizers alternate on the grid like a checker
board.

The code was first constructed on a torus where there are no boundaries. Since this
topology isn’t implementable experimentally, we present the bounded surface code. The
rounded 2-qubit stabilizers are added to create boundaries for the code. There are two
types of boundaries: Z-boundaries with Z-type 2-qubit stabilizers, and X-boundaries with
the X-type 2-qubit stabilizers.

This surface code encodes a single logical qubit. Considering the Z-boundaries to be
associated to Z-type stabilizers, the logical operator Zℓ connects both Z-boundaries. This
is because the Z Pauli string needs to commute with all stabilizers, so it must have even
overlap with all X-type stabilizers. It is possible if the strings connects the 2-qubit Z-type
stabilizers, or in other words if it connects both Z-boundaries. In figure 3.4, we illustrate a
representative that goes along the bottom X-boundary. Any other Pauli string equivalent
to this one up to stabilizers is also a logical Z operator. Similarly, Xℓ connects the two
X-boundaries, so it lies along the Z-boundary. The code distance, which corresponds to

identical X and Z-type stabilizers. From this argument, one would suspect that self-dual

additional phase is adds another constraint: since it has a period of 4, the weight of the
stabilizers must respect w(si) = 0 (mod 4) for all si the in the group. So doubly even
self-dual CSS codes have transversal S gates [61].

Looking at the bulk stabilizers, one might think the surface is a doubly even code,

complicated than simply transversal and non-transversal gates, and we will address this
in subsection 3.3.5. For now, know that the FT protocols for the S gate don’t create the
same bottlenecks as for non-Clifford gates.

With a new sense of paranoia, we revisit the transversality of H gate. By looking
at the symmetry of the surface code patch in figure 3.4, one can notice that Hadamard
gates applied transversally maps the stabilizers to each other up to a geometrical 90◦ rota-
tion. This does not affect the information badly, meaning the H gate is truly transversal.
However, a protocol to rotate the surface code is needed to make it compatible for future
lattice surgery protocols with neighbouring logical qubits [97]. It simply requires grow the
code patch by measuring stabilizers with neighbouring qubits and measure out some of the
qubits such that the code rotates [99, Fig. 1]. These types of operations are called code
deformation.

The transversal CNOT is implemented by applying CNOTs between all pairs of qubits
between two blocks of surface code. While CNOTs between qubits within a code block can
spread errors in a non-FT way, here the CNOT connects qubits in different code blocks.
If an error spreads from one code block to the other, it remains correctable for both code
blocks individually.

While this is exactly what we are looking for in theory, in practice it may be diffi-
cult to implement. Many quantum computer architectures only have nearest neighbour
interactions, such as superconducting quantum computers whose qubits lay on a chip. So
operations that require the whole code block to move around may be out of reach. This is
where lattice surgery comes in.

3.3.6 Contributions and Outlooks

The underlying FT protocol to perform a CNOT was proposed by Gottesman [131], but it
was Horsman et al. [17] that found a circuit-level implementation of this idea for surface
codes that respects the constraints of superconducting quantum computers: 2D layout and
nearest neighbour interactions.

Following this work, lattice surgery was optimized such that it overshadows other con-
curring techniques such as braiding in terms of efficiency [128]. The state injection protocols
were also improved upon by using twist defects [132, 133] and then optimized [134] allowing
the |Yℓ⟩ state to be produced by classical updates of basis, making it trivially FT. Finally,
lattice surgery may be generalized to QLDPC codes [135], and improved by looking at
these schemes from a gauge fixing perspective [136].

The simplest way to generate logical Clifford gates is through code automorphisms. Here,
logical gates are generated using single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations, such
that the resulting gates are transversal.

Given a unitary operator U acting on the encoded state |ψℓ⟩ associated with the sta-
bilizer group S, then its action on the encoded state can be mapped to its action on the

While code automorphisms are useful because of their inherent FT properties, they can’t
give the full logical n-qubit Clifford group [126]. This raises the need to go beyond this
simple tool. While we can look to magic state injection or lattice surgery (for certain codes),
in this section we introduce a new paradigm based on dynamical codes: the measurement
sequence induced by the dynamical code may generate logic, all while measuring relevant
information for decoding. [28, 38]. In other words, the logical information may go beyond
the base code and into other codes in order to perform logical gates.

This idea was first explored by Paetznick and Reichardt [28], where they use a [[15, 7, 3]]
Hamming code [25] and use 6 qubits as gauge qubits to generate a H gate. This is because
the H⊗15 applied to the code may have a nontrivial action on a gauge qubit. This can be
corrected by measuring their Z operators and performing a bit flip if necessary. Since these
codes have a transversal CCZ gate [25], this generates the full universal gate set [141].

This concept, at its simplest, has been further explored in the form of code switching,
first suggested by Anderson et al. [142]. As the name indicates, this groups procedures
that transfer information from a base code into another code. The goal of switching to
another code is to access its set of transversal gates, so the two codes are chosen such that
their respective sets of transversal gates form a universal gate set.

In their work, Anderson et al. explain a code switching procedure between the Steane’s
7-qubit code [85] and the 15-qubit Reed-Muller code (see Table 3.1), which are respectively
the smallest 2D and 3D colour codes. Their work highlights that these two codes have a
parent subsystem code, so code switching may be seen as gauge fixing. As mentioned in
section 3.2.2, the latter has a transversal non-Clifford, while the Steane code has the rest
of the single-qubit Clifford gates transversally [119, 143]. The code switching between the
2D and 3D colour codes has been generalized to larger code size and dimensions [29, 30].

code switching need not necessarily be implemented through gauge fixing in order to
be fault-tolerant. In fact, it is possible to convert the 5-qubit code (figure 2.5) and the
Steane 7-qubit code discussed above in a FT way using 2-qubit gates [144], even if 2-qubit
gates within the same code patch are generally prohibited in FTQC. This technique is
called code deformation. However, these can be replaced by gauge fixing [1], so we will not
further expand on it.

code switching has more to offer than going back and forth between two codes. In
fact, it is possible to find a sequence of gauge fixings that connects any two stabilizer codes
[145]. Dynamical automorphisms (DAs) [38] generalize this idea in order to explore a bigger

qubit Clifford gates, qubit permutations and measurements. The tool used to navigate the
space is gauge fixing, implemented through measurement, which connects codes that have
common parent subsystem codes. We summarize the scheme proposed in figure 3.6.

We allow ourselves measurements, rather than 2-qubit Clifford gates, because the mea-
surement circuits may be more easily made fault-tolerant. Fault-tolerant Pauli measure-
ments are non-destructive. Instead of measuring the physical qubits themselves, the de-
sired information is transferred through CNOTs onto ancilla qubits that are measured
[114]. While the CNOTs may cause bad error propagation as highlighted in Section 3.1,
since the ancilla qubits are not part of the code block, this can be more easily mitigated.
These types of circuits were first studied in the context of syndrome measurements [119,
146–148]. The current standard technique makes use of flag qubits[149, 150], extra ancilla
qubits that catch potential errors in the measurement circuit. It is important to note that
high weight measurements may be reduced decomposed into a sequence of smaller weight
operators [151], making their FT circuits more easily realizable.

After this detour on measurement circuits, we go back to DAs proposed by Davydova
et al. They develop a formalism to describe DAs based on the anyon perspective. In fact,
there exists a subfield of QEC where topological codes, such as the stabilizer code and the
colour code, are seen as anyon models. While an important part of the literature, this
approach to QEC is beyond the scope of this manuscript. Instead, we will look at gauge
fixing in the stabilizer tableau formalism (subsection 2.3.5) and the ZX-calculus perspective

67



(chapter 4).

The authors give an example of a FT DA for the colour code based on 2-qubit mea-
surements and give the decoding procedure for it. By using the 3D colour code, which has
a transversal non-Clifford gate, they are able to create a DA implementing a non-Clifford
gate. In general, DAs are not expected to implement non-Clifford gates because they are
procedures represented with the stabilizer formalism, which is in the Clifford fragment,
meaning it may be represented as Clifford circuits [15].

That being said, the authors don’t offer a general approach to building DAs for other
codes. Furthermore, it remains unclear how to systematically build DAs where the logical
information is guaranteed to be stay protected throughout the procedure, as it does in the
colour code example they give.

Dynamical automorphisms are based on measurements of gauge operators to implement
gauge fixing, so one might think they are in the category of measurement-based quantum
computing [152]. There exists a mapping between them [37], but these two schemes are
very different in spirit. The former uses dynamical logical qubits in order to implement
logical gates in a QEC protected way. The latter uses cluster states with n × D qubits
to represent circuits with n physical qubits and D time steps, where the single qubit
measurements are consumed to perform the logical operations of the circuit.

Chapter 4

Dynamical Automorphisms via the
ZX-Calculus

Brief introduction for the paper and the content that will be discussed more in details

The ZX-calculus is a graphical language for reasoning about quantum circuits, which
has recently found many applications in quantum error correction.

Here, we develop a formalism based on the ZX-calculus that enables us to design dynam-
ical automorphisms for stabilizer codes. This method is based on gauge fixing, in which
measurements are used to switch between different stabilizer codes. We combine gauge
fixing steps to implement a loop in the space of stabilizer codes, returning to the original
codespace with a logical Clifford gate applied. We find gauge fixing acts as “chutes and lad-
ders” between different encodings of stabilizer codes, enabling dynamical automorphisms.
This work provides three examples of such logical gates, including a distance-preserving
phase gate for a code whose code automorphisms generate no non-trivial action. We
conclude by suggesting a machine-interpretable method for constructing dynamical auto-
morphisms and facilitates the search for implementations of desired logical gates.

4.2 Dynamical Automorphisms and ZX-encoding graphs

As seen in the previous section, gauge fixing can be leveraged to transfer the logical infor-
mation from one stabilizer code to another. In fact, logical gates such as lattice surgery
and code switching can be understood as gauge fixing [99, 155]. As a reminder, dynamical
automorphism gates [38] can be understood as a generalization of code switching where
we perform local Clifford gates, qubit permutations and gauge fixings from one stabilizer
to another until we return to the original code, up to a logical gate. In other words, dy-
namical automorphisms are produced by nontrivial loops in the space of [[n, k]] stabilizer
codes. Since we know that any two codes can be connected with high probability in a
distance-preserving way via code switching [156, theorem 1] (see also [145, section 2.6] and
[155]), this space is rich and can be used as a resource.

As an introduction, we begin with a motivating example using a [[3, 1]] code. This
example illustrates how one can achieve a logical action using a single gauge fixing. Then,
we look at a gauge fixing that entangles logical qubits in the [[4, 2, 2]] code. We move on to
a more meaningful example with the [[7, 1, 3]] code, where the gauge fixings are distance-
preserving and the logical gate is not generated by its code automorphism group. We end
this section by generalizing the idea to logical 2-qubit Clifford gates, and suggesting a way
to find a gauge fixing procedure generating a given Clifford logical gate.

4.2.5 Generalization to Logical 2-Qubit Cliffords

So far, we have explored the application of building a subsystem code that gauge fixes into
the original stabilizer code. In general, subsystem codes will gauge fix into three different
stabilizer codes. We would like to leverage these as bridges in the [[n, k]] stabilizer code
space in order find a systematic method to look for 2-qubit Clifford gates. However, the
search space can be immense, especially when adding more qubits, i.e. more vertices in the

Chapter 5

Discussion and Conclusion

We started this thesis by introducing in chapter 2 some quantum information basics, the
stabilizer formalism and the ZX-calculus. First, we defined quantum states, quantum chan-
nels and two representations, the Choi representation and the Kraus representation. This
then enabled us to lay the bases of the stabilizer formalism. In particular, we introduced
Pauli operators, Clifford gates, non-Clifford gates and the symplectic representation, as
well as stabilizer states and graph states. The next step was to discuss stabilizer codes.
We built up to subsystem codes, gauge fixing and dynamical codes, which are at the centre
of this manuscript. However, there was still a big chunk missing: the ZX-calculus. We
first defined this graphical language and its connection to graph states before representing
stabilizer codes in it using ZX-encoding graphs. We also explored different properties of
these objects that were necessary to understand the results like the LC equivalence, their
associated stabilizer tableau, and their normal form.

Before delving into the results, we first reviewed some fault-tolerant methods to build
logic in stabilizer codes in chapter 3. First, we defined fault-tolerant gates as mapping
correctable errors to each other. We also defined transversal gates. Next, we introduced
the first FT protocol, magic state distillation. It is a protocol to generate high-fidelity
non-Clifford gates using many noisy states to make good magic states. Then, we looked at
lattice surgery, a technique to realize fault-tolerant CNOTs in the surface code and QLDPC
codes. After two complex protocols, we fell back on code automorphisms, which are a type
transversal gates based on LC gates and qubit permutation. Finally, we considered adding
measurements as a tool for logic in dynamical automorphisms. In DAs, a gauge fixing
sequence projects logical information onto different codespaces until it gets back to the
original encoding, generating a logical Clifford gate along the way.

90



In chapter 4, we discussed the results of this work: dynamical automorphisms via the
ZX-calculus. We first introduce gauge fixing in the ZX-calculus. In particular, we define a
gauge qubit in ZX-encoding graphs as an input of the graph. Thus, gauge fixing becomes
the act of closing off the input with a Z, X or Y eigenstate, represented by a red spider with
a different LC gate attached. We then explained how the action of gauge fixing projects the
subsystem code into different codespaces, depending on the choice of gauge fixing. After, it
became natural to consider building the ZX-encoding graph of a subsystem code from the
ZX-encoding graph of the stabilizer code it gauge fixes. This may be achieved by carefully
adding a gauge input, and we define it as extending the ZX-encoding graph. We go on
to prove that it is in fact possible to build any and all ZX-encoding graphs of subsystem
codes which gauge fix into a given ZX-encoding graph by extending it. Our proof relies
on the fact the normal form of a ZX-encoding graph is unique. We also give an alternate
proof using a counting argument. Finally, we compare gauge fixing via the ZX-calculus to
the familiar stabilizer tableau formalism. We thus confirm with an example that these two
formalisms for gauge fixing are equivalent.

Having defined gauge fixing via the ZX-calculus, we then used it as a tool to generate
logic through dynamical automorphisms. We first explored a simple example with a 3-qubit
motivating code, where the logical gate realized was outside the set of gates generated by
code automorphisms. This showed that dynamical automorphisms do have an edge over
code automorphisms. However, it was a bit peculiar that a single gauge fixing step was
sufficient to generate a nontrivial action, considering that dynamical automorphisms are
nontrivial loops in the space of stabilizer codes. To understand this, we looked at the
LC orbit of the code, and found that the gauge fixing was acting like chutes and ladders
between different encodings of the same stabilizer code. So the loop was hidden inside
the LC orbit. Then, we moved on to 2-qubit Clifford gates. We gave an example of a
dynamical automorphism implementing a logical CZ gate for the [[4, 2, 2]] code. Again,
a single gauge fixing was sufficient in this protocol, the making the procedure distance-
preserving. Finally, we looked at distance-preserving dynamical automorphism for the
([[7, 1, 3]]) bare code, where the logical qubit was projected onto different stabilizer codes
before coming back to the original space up to a phase gate. Interestingly, this gate was
also cannot be generated via the code automorphism group.

Now that we understand better our formalism, we can compare it to the other FT
protocols reviewed in chapter 3. First, since our formalism is based on the Clifford fragment
of the ZX-calculus, it cannot describe any non-Clifford gates. As such, it is complementary
to magic state distillation. However, if we choose our base code to be a triorthogonal code
[25] which has a transversal non-Clifford gate, then we would bypass the need for magic
state distillation.

91



Second, we point out that lattice surgery, presented in Section 3.3, and code deformation
can be thought of as gauge fixing [99]. So our gauge fixing formalism could be used to
describe lattice surgery as well as dynamical automorphisms. Also, we point out that
latticed surgery has been described in the ZX-calculus [127]. The results presented in
Chapter 4 are thus close in flavour to this prior work. Our work differentiates itself because
they look at the procedures on the logical level, whereas we create a gauge fixing formalism,
giving measurement schedules for the physical qubits.

Finally, the examples of dynamical automorphisms for the 3-qubit code and the bare
code presented in section 4.2 are clear examples that code automorphisms are weaker than
dynamical automorphisms. However, the latter require more complex protocols because
of the gauge operator measurements. Because our formalism uses compact graph-like ZX-
diagrams, it loses information about the physical implementation of these gauge fixings.
One could imagine using ZX-calculus rules to extract measurement circuits from the ZX-
encoding graphs. It would be interesting to take inspiration from distance-preserving
rewrites in the ZX-calculus [54] to obtain distance-preserving measurement circuits.

An important extension of our work is to compute the effect of the gauge fixing steps
on the code distance, which may decrease in some cases [99]. To accurately benchmark the
performance of our dynamical automorphism gates, we would also need to construct circuits
for measuring the gauge operators and include rounds of stabilizer measurement. Before
reaching these next steps, we do not have enough information to compare FT protocols
based on dynamical automorphisms to magic state distillation or lattice surgery.

One of the strong suits of the formalism is that ZX-encoding graphs can be stored bit
wise using the Nauty package for graphs [154]. Then, local complementations and thus
LC gates correspond to bit wise operations, which are very efficient. This would make the
breadth-first scheme discussed in subsection 4.2.5 also potentially efficient. One issue that
might arise is the data processing. As the number of physical and logical qubits grows,
the bigger the space of [[n, k]] stabilizer codes get. So managing the data from all the LC
orbits of the codes and all the subsystems may be hard in practice.

Also, the formalism is very intuitive: it is straightforward to see when a logical gate
appears after some gauge fixings. So when considering bigger codes, it would be interesting
to see if an AI model could also understand these diagrams intuitively [161]. It also may
be able detect patterns to predict when gauge fixings are distance-preserving, helping to
direct the search towards fault-tolerant dynamical automorphisms.

abstracts.value:
Quantum error correction enables the protection of quantum information from noise arising from imperfect control and unwanted interactions with the environment. Manipulating logical information in quantum error-correcting codes remains challenging, as we can only directly access physical qubits, not the encoded logical qubits. In fact, we know it is not possible to get the full logical universal gate set by doing transversal physical operations. As a solution to this problem, many schemes for implementing encoded logical gates have been developed, including dynamical automorphism gates (DA). These logical protocols are realized by measurement sequences that transfer logical information between different codespaces. In parallel, there has been a growing interest in the intersection between quantum error correction and the ZX-calculus, a graphical representation of quantum processes. This direction has proved to be fruitful. For example, it has allowed the development of new dynamical codes. However, logic within such codes has not yet been tackled. In this thesis, we offer a formalism for dynamical automorphisms based on the ZX-calculus, implementing logical Clifford gates for stabilizer codes. We begin by defining the basics of quantum information, the stabilizer formalism and the ZX-calculus. Then, we build upon this formalism for gauge fixing via the ZX-calculus. Since gauge fixing may be implemented via measurement, our formalism allows us to protocols implementing dynamical automorphisms. In particular, we start by investigating a DA for a 3-qubit motivating code and its LC orbit. Then, we turn to an example of a logical CZ for the [[4, 2, 2]]code. Finally, we show an example of a distance-preserving dynamical automorphism for the [[7, 1, 3]] bare code implementing a phase gate, which was inaccessible using previous
techniques.

Abstract

Italian version

Con questo lavoro di tesi si presenta lo studio di metodi per ottenere modelli di rumore
equivalenti per misure dirette a due qubit e l’applicazione di essi a piattaforme supercon-
duttive in regime dispersivo. L’interesse in tale argomento è dovuto al fatto che di recente
sono stati pubblicati codici di correzione degli errori detti Floquet codes o dynamical
codes che sfruttano queste misure di parità a peso due codificando i qubit in maniera
dinamica. L’obiettivo era dunque capire come queste misure potessero indurre errori e
testare come questi codici di correzione reagissero al modello. I metodi sono stati stu-
diati e applicati ad un particolare tipo di errore semplificato che consiste in un dephasing
all’interno del sottospazio di parità pari di un sistema a due qubit, dopodichè il modello
è stato implementato in un simulatore per il calcolo della soglia in funzione dell’ampiezza
del segnale di ingresso al risonatore di readout.

English version

With this thesis work we present the study of methods to obtain equivalent error models
for direct two-qubit parity measurements and their applications to superconducting plat-
forms in dispersive regime. The interest in this topic is due to recently published error
correcting codes called Floquet codes or dynamical codes that use these weight-2 parity
measurements to encode dynamical qubits. The goal was then to understand how these
measurements could induce errors and benchmark how these dynamical codes respond to
the error model. The methods have been studied and applied to a particular simplified
error consisting in an even-parity subspace dephasing for a two-qubit system and we ob-
tained a threshold simulation as a function of the amplitude of the signal applied to the
resonator in the readout phase.

Introduction

Since the first ideas proposed by Richard P. Feynman [7] in 1982 regarding the hint to
build quantum machines to unlock new methods to simulate quantum systems, scientists
and engineers from all over the world started developing theories and experiments to pre-
dict or verify the capabilities of these machines called quantum computers. There are a
lot of results showing that quantum machines can perform specific tasks with even expo-
nentially lower complexity compared to the classical counterpart thanks to the so-called
quantum parallelism. For example the factorization of prime numbers with a quantum
computer is possible within an exponentially faster algorithm called Shor’s algorithm [31]
or binary search in a database can be performed quadratically faster thanks to Grover’s
algorithm [11]. This led to waves of enthusiasm in the field and researchers became eager
to find new fast algorithms and applications for the quantum speed-up obtained with a
set of known algorithms. These applications can go from drug discovery and forecast
predictions to logistics, finance and much more.

Regarding the best candidates to host physical realizations of quantum computers,
there are for example superconducting platforms, neutral atoms and semiconductor qubits
but many other platforms are being developed like topological qubits engineering Majo-
rana bound states. All these platforms have their strong features and weaknesses but one
single thing is common to all of them: quantum processes are extremely weak against
noise and so this implies the necessity of quantum error correcting codes to reach a point
where these technologies can become scalable and useful.

This thesis stands in the middle between the physics of superconducting platforms
and quantum error correcting codes, so first of all we will introduce the reader to the
needed concepts of quantum error correction in chapter 1 and quantum electrodynamics
of superconducting circuits in chapter 2; then an overview on open quantum systems for
error models will be presented in chapter 3 and in the end – in chapter 4 – all the knowledge
will be gathered in a workflow from a master equation that describes the interactions in
the quantum system to an equivalent stochastic channel that models the errors. Studying
error models of physical platforms is very important in modern quantum computing for
two reasons: first of all we can benchmark existing quantum error correcting codes to see
how they perform when trying to correct these errors, then it is also extremely important
to know the errors happening in a platform because it can lead to the design of error-aware
error correcting codes made ad hoc for the particular physical realization. In this project
we chose to mix the construction of a model and to observe how a new class of quantum
error correcting codes called Floquet codes [13] perform with the specific error model we
developed.

1





Chapter 1

Quantum Error Correction

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) can be considered as the branch of Quantum Informa-
tion Theory that studies how to contrast decoherence and correct the undesired evolution
of (open) quantum systems. The concepts of this chapter are inspired by the contents of
[26], [32], [25] and [2]. We recommend the reader to check Appendices A, B, C and D to
ensure you have most of the knowledge needed to understand the topics of this chapter.

1.1 Basic concepts

Quantum states are encoded using a (usually large) number of redundant qubits. This
abundance of non-logically needed dimensions will help us to preserve the information
contained in k logical qubits encoded in the total n-qubit system.

Definition 1.1.1 ([26]). Let H = (C2)⊗n be the total Hilbert space that describes the
n-qubit system. We define a quantum error correcting code as a subspace C ⊆ H.

Error correction operations are performed periodically to minimize (in principle an-
nihilate) the continuous degradation of quantum information caused by a certain error
E . The whole procedure of error correction (detection followed by recovery) is usually
performed measuring some observables, whose eigenvalues are called error syndromes β,
and then applying a proper error recovery operator R(β) that can evolve the state back
to the original code space C, hopefully removing the error. An error correcting cycle can
be then summarized starting from a state |ϕ⟩ ∈ C through the following steps:

|ϕ⟩ External noise E−−−−−−−−−→ |ϕ′⟩ Syndrome measurement−−−−−−−−−−−−−→ β
Syndrome recovery R−−−−−−−−−−−−→ |ϕ⟩

The recovery operator R and usually (but not always) the noise model E are trace pre-
serving quantum operation.
To get a successful error correcting cycle we must impose that for all density operators ρ
whose support is the code space C:

(R ◦ E)(ρ) ∝ ρ (1.1)

where the proportionality symbol is used instead of the equality symbol because E can be
a non-trace preserving quantum operation. Equation 1.1 is the starting point to determine
the properties that our quantum error correcting code must satisfy such as the following
